name: Go Bag Checklist
description: A grab-and-go evacuation bag, packed in advance for the moment there is no time to think.

sections.title: Documents (copies, sealed in a waterproof bag)

items.text: Passports, driving licences and birth certificates
Insurance policies: home, car, health, life
Deeds, lease or mortgage papers
Bank and credit card details
A printed list of emergency contacts
items.note: Written on paper, because a dead phone takes your contacts with it.

items.text: Medical records, allergies and prescriptions
A USB drive with scans of everything above
Recent photos of family members and pets
items.note: Used to identify them if you are separated.

items.text: One litre of water per person, plus a filter or purification tablets
Three days of food that needs no cooking
A manual can opener if any of it is tinned
Food for any dietary restriction in the household
items.note: Shelters rarely cater for allergies or infant formula.

items.text: Seven days of every prescription medicine
A written list of medicines with doses and prescriber
First aid kit with bandages, antiseptic and painkillers
Spare glasses, contact lenses and solution
Hearing aid batteries or other device spares
Diary a date to rotate anything with an expiry
items.note: Set a calendar reminder every six months; this is the step that gets skipped.

items.text: Power bank, charged, plus cables for every device
Hand-crank or battery radio
Torch and spare batteries
Whistle
Paper map of the area with two routes out marked
items.note: Phone navigation fails when the network is down or towers burn.

items.text: Cash in small notes
items.note: Card readers need power and a network; neither is reliable in an evacuation.

items.text: Spare house and car keys
A written note of where the household will meet
One change of clothing per person
Sturdy closed shoes
Rain jacket or poncho
Emergency blanket or sleeping bag
Work gloves
N95 masks
items.note: Smoke and demolition dust are the common hazards after a fire or quake.

sections.title: People who need their own bag

items.text: Infants: formula, bottles, nappies, wipes
Children: one comfort item each
items.note: Small thing, large difference on the first night away.

items.text: Older adults: mobility aids, spare batteries, care plan
Pets: carrier, lead, food, vaccination records
Store the bag where you can reach it without going upstairs
Tell everyone in the house where it is
Recharge the power bank every few months
Review the whole bag twice a year
Re-cut it as children grow or medication changes

faq.q: What is the difference between a go bag and an emergency kit?
faq.a: A go bag is carried out of the house during an evacuation and holds what you need for the first 72 hours away. An emergency kit stays home and supports you sheltering in place. Many households keep both, with documents and medication duplicated in the go bag.

faq.q: How much water should a go bag hold?
faq.a: About one litre per person is the practical limit before the bag becomes too heavy to carry, so pair it with a filter or purification tablets rather than trying to carry three days of drinking water.

faq.q: Where should the go bag be kept?
faq.a: By the door you would actually leave through, or in the car if you are likely to drive out. Anywhere that needs stairs or a search is too far — the bag is useless if you cannot reach it in the minutes you have.

faq.q: How often should it be checked?
faq.a: Twice a year is the usual rhythm, tied to something you already remember such as clock changes. Check expiry dates on food, water and medication, recharge the power bank, and swap children's clothing for the current size.
